I do think that a quick rules overview is useful, but far too many reviews seem to try to cover the whole rulebook. Also, many use a single camera somewhat far back, so the components are hard to see (especially text on cards). When going over the components, I think an improvement to most reviews is to see what the better toy reviewers do when they're showing the details/articulation on toys.

But the one aspect that I truly find missing from current reviews is that the "what I think" segment of the review seems to always be the reviewer just talking to the camera. When my friends and I play a game, and we like or hate something, it's something that is best demonstrated with the game itself, and has to do with the rules. I really wish the criticisms were more tied into the rules explanation.

Oddly enough, the best example of what I would like to see more of isn't from a board game reviewer, and was a review about how brutal the Pokemon Master Trainer board game was.

I know this is a missed rule example, but here goes. I introduced one of my friends to Pandemic and he was instantly hooked. Next time I talked to him, he had gotten the game and played it with his father and brother - he told me he found the game a bit too easy.’x as he was winning no problem. We talked a bit back and forth, and we decided to have a game ourselves. During an epidemic we got hit by a chain reaction outbreak, and I applied it - he was shocked “why are you doing that?”. Well it is in the rules, I told him. He refused to believe me, so we looked up the rules and he agreed I was right. I then told him that was most likely why he thought the game was easy - when we spoke later on he told me Pandemic was harder than he thought - sorry for the long post, just came to me.

It's amazing how much strategy you can actually cram into such a simple rule-set. And it explains itself in such a short amount of time, too (Every turn, you play your card, place houses on tiles of the cards type, then draw a new card. Houses must be adjacent to other houses of your own if possible. There are these abilities on the field [explain abilities], and castles are worth 3 points. These cards determine score. Any questions? Okay, a quick note on strategy: being able to spread out and leaving yourself with options on where to place your settlements is key to having a good time, so movement abilities are really good, and placing your initial settlements in ways that minimizes the chance you'll have to place adjacent next turn is a huge help. Not OP, but it's basically Twilight Struggle (shared designer) without any risk of defcon suicides. Players play as either Nixon or JFK. It's a bit lighter than TS, but still with a lot of moving parts.  Opponent's cards' actions have to be activated manually by opponent (using 'momentum markers' resource) or can be blocked entirely using your own momentum markers.  Thus drawing a bad hand for a ~~round~~ turn isn't quite as devastating as in TS.  I prefer 1960 over TS because I find it less stressful.

I try to base it off ideas and not a number. What I mean is, I'm willing to keep trying a game I didn't enjoy as long as I have so new idea about how to approach it, a new strategy to try, etc. If I'm not having fun and go through more than 1 playthrough without an idea of how to play it in a different way, that's when I'll lose interest.

It could be the second or third play of a new game, but I've also played things I didn't like necessarily off the bat a bunch because I had a new idea to try.

Maybe it's because I enjoy exploration to some base amount, so I can find exploring the game more fun than actually playing it.
